title: Netflix's Musafir Cafe Has Viewers Hunting for a Real Cafe in Uttarakhand
excerpt: Vikrant Massey's romantic drama, set in Mussoorie's misty hills, has sparked a wave of fans searching for the show's mountain cafe — but the truth is more complicated than a Google Maps pin.
body:
• Netflix's Musafir Cafe, starring Vikrant Massey, was filmed on location in Mussoorie and Bhopal but the titular cafe is a fictional set built for the show.
  • Real cafes called Musafir Cafe exist in Uttarakhand towns like Kotdwar and Rishikesh, though they have no connection to the series.
  • The show marks Massey's debut as a producer through his banner Homemade Stories, and is based on Divya Prakash Dubey's bestselling Hindi novel.
  • Viewers have flooded social media asking for the cafe's location, underscoring the show's success at building an emotionally authentic hill-station world.

Within days of its July 24 premiere on Netflix, Vikrant Massey's romantic drama Musafir Cafe triggered an unexpected side effect: thousands of viewers started searching Google Maps for the cafe's real address. Set against the misty hills of Mussoorie, the show presents its titular coffee shop with such lived-in warmth — earthy interiors, handwritten menus, carefully brewed pour-overs — that audiences assumed they could drive up and order a cup.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=CY603P-PeQQ

They can't. The Musafir Cafe depicted in the series is a fictional establishment, a set designed specifically for the show. No cafe in Mussoorie carries the name or shares the history shown on screen.

The Fiction That Felt Too Real

That so many viewers believed the cafe exists is a testament to the production's attention to detail. Director Ruchir Arun, known for the understated intimacy of Little Things, shot extensively on location in Mussoorie and Bhopal, blending real hill-station scenery with constructed interiors. The cafe set was designed to feel like a place audiences had already visited — complete with regulars who treat it like a second home and mountain views visible from every window.

"We are all made of love stories. Some we chase, some that find us, some that make us travel, and some that make us brave."

— Musafir Cafe production team, in Netflix's announcement

Within the story, the cafe embodies the dream of its protagonist, Chander Mohan Sharma (Massey) — a restless software engineer who quits his logistics career to build something meaningful in the mountains. The name "Musafir," meaning traveller, was suggested by Sudha (Vedika Pinto), the woman Chander fell for during an arranged-marriage meeting in Bhopal years earlier. The cafe he eventually opens with his wife Preeti (Mahima Makwana) carries that earlier love's fingerprints on every detail.

Real Musafir Cafes Do Exist — Just Not This One

Adding to the confusion: Uttarakhand actually has several cafes named Musafir. In Kotdwar, along the road to Lansdowne, a Musafir Cafe has operated for years, earning a 4.7-star rating on Google from nearly 150 reviews. In Rishikesh's Laxman Jhula area, Mastana Musafir Cafe has built a cult following among backpackers. A third Musafir Cafe operates in Dehradun, open from 6 AM to 10:30 PM daily.

None have any connection to the Netflix series. The name "musafir" — traveller — is a natural fit for cafes in a state synonymous with pilgrimage routes, trekking trails and spiritual journeys. But the show's popularity has likely sent a surge of curious visitors toward these real-life namesakes.

Massey's Dual Bet: Actor and Producer

Musafir Cafe carries extra significance as the first project from Homemade Stories, Massey's newly launched production banner. After winning the National Film Award for Best Actor for 12th Fail (shared with Shah Rukh Khan) and announcing a brief career hiatus in late 2024, Massey returned with a project that stakes his reputation on both sides of the camera.

The series is produced in partnership with Terribly Tiny Tales (TTT), the digital storytelling platform co-founded by Anuj Gosalia. It adapts Divya Prakash Dubey's 2016 Hindi novel of the same name, a modern romance that struck a chord with young urban Indian readers for its grounded take on love, arranged marriages and the gap between passion and companionship.

The cast includes Adil Hussain as Mark Abraham, a philosophical older figure who guides Chander's emotional journey, along with Rajeev Siddhartha, Anubha Fatehpuria, Loveleen Mishra and Sadia Siddiqui in supporting roles. Dubey himself makes a cameo appearance.

Critical Reception and the Mussoorie Effect

Reviews have praised the show's restrained tone. Decider called it a "stream it," noting its "relaxed vibe" and favourable comparisons to Virgin River and This Is Us. Vedika Pinto's performance as Sudha — a fiercely independent divorce attorney — has drawn particular attention. The eight-episode first season runs 35 to 42 minutes per episode, moving between two timelines: Chander and Sudha's electric connection eight years ago in Bhopal, and the present-day life Chander has built with Preeti in Mussoorie.

"Vedika Pinto infuses Sudha with a fierceness and a sense of fun that we don't tend to see in Indian dramas."

— Joel Keller, Decider

For viewers in the diaspora, the show taps into a familiar ache: the romanticised pull of India's hill stations, the idea that somewhere in the mountains exists a perfect cafe where life slows down enough to make sense. That the cafe doesn't exist has done nothing to blunt the fantasy — it may have sharpened it.

What's Next

Netflix has not announced a second season, though the first season's ending leaves several threads open. If real-world interest is any measure of appetite, the show has already achieved something rare: making a fictional address feel like a destination. Whether Massey's production gamble extends to a follow-up season may depend on viewership numbers over the coming weeks — and on how many travellers actually show up in Mussoorie looking for a coffee shop that exists only on screen.
nri_angle: The show taps into the diaspora's romanticised longing for Indian hill-station life and the idea of escaping to a simpler world in the mountains.
